v.why: At low LR with a fixed 243-epoch budget, a smaller batch gives many more Adam updates and relieves undertraining.
sklearn divides the L2 term by batch size, so a larger batch weakens the effective penalty under high alpha and relieves underfitting.
Very wide networks overfit and have redundant capacity that L2 can usefully shrink.
L2 sums over all weights, so widening increases the total penalty under strong alpha and pushes the net toward underfitting.
A single hidden layer relies on width for all of its capacity, so widening substitutes for the missing depth.
At low LR a wider net moves further in function space per step because many units shift in aggregate, offsetting the small step size.
Narrow layers can be compensated by composing more of them, so added depth substitutes for missing width.
Deeper nets at high LR suffer compounded updates and exploding or dead ReLU activations.
Large batches give few updates in the fixed epoch budget, so a larger LR compensates for undertraining and is safe given low gradient noise.
Wide layers already take large effective steps, so raising the LR overshoots and kills ReLUs.
